raw_data.analysis:
An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code. The attacker would need to specially craft a malicious RTF document file and convince a user to open it. The application may crash during the exploitation attempt resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

 

A detailed write-up outlining the creation of a malicious RTF file is available online. Minimal effort is required to create such an RTF file, which would be executed automatically upon opening the OLE object. In the example it launches a hidden powershell process to connect with Metasploit.

 

Exploit code was released in the form of a Python script. The script acts as a toolkit that can generate a malicious RTF file and host an HTA file on a local instance of Apache Web server for OLE linking in the malicious RTF. User interaction is still required to open the malicious RTF file.

 

Further, a Metasploit module has been added to the Metasploit Framework. The module is capable of creating a specially crafted RTF file. When downloaded and opened or previewed in Microsoft Office products, the vulnerability is triggered and an embedded payload is executed.

 

Exploitation activity was previously reported as being observed in the wild. In addition to that exploitation, FireEye has identified an exploit document which was uploaded from Brazil. It is believed that this document was used to attack Brazil according to it"s submission country and decoy file contents. Upon execution, this malicious file downloads more malicious Macros samples from an external link. The Macros files launches PowerShell commands, which in turn, injects the Revenge RAT malware into a victim"s system.

 

FireEye has recently identified a malicious document that we suspect could have been used to target Argentinian victims. Upon exploitation, it drops a REMCOS RAT (Remote Administration Tool) on a vulnerable host, allowing an attacker to control a victim"s machine.

 

Another malicious .doc file has been identified by FireEye which contains an exploit that is reportedly being used to install Revenge RAT Malware on victim machines. Upon execution, the exploit communicates with a C&C server hosted on a Brazilian IP (187.14.228.49). The Revenge RAT Malware would allow an attacker to remotely control a victimized machine.

 

Actor JackDelta has been reportedly selling an Office Word Exploit Builder with subscription services on multiple hacking related forums under different but similar handlers and posts.

 

Pakistani-linked threat actor APT36 has reportedly exploited this vulnerability as part of an email phishing campaign to distribute Crimson RAT. This campaign has made use of false COVID-19 health advisories that claim to originate from the government of India, with attached Microsoft Office documents containing a Visual Basic payload.

 

Chinese-linked threat actor APT10 has reportedly exploited this vulnerability in conjunction with several others in targeted attacks against government institutions, cloud service providers, and customer networks worldwide.

 

In June 2021, Mandiant observed exploitation of this vulnerability in-the-wild as part of a malicious RTF document containing the POISONSTEEL .NET backdoor as a payload.

 

In October 2021, Mandiant observed exploitation of this vulnerability in the wild as part of a malicious .doc file containing an unidentified dropper.

 

In April 2022, Mandiant observed evidence of exploitation by the DPRK against South Korean targets, making use of malicious .docx files with a Visual Basic payload.

 

Microsoft reportedly addressed this vulnerability in an update. FireEye considers this a High-risk vulnerability due to the potential for arbitrary code execution of a known zero day vulnerability currently being exploited in the wild. Though the vulnerability requires user interaction, it is still being considered High-risk due to the current exploitation activity.

 
 


CISA added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on November 3, 2021, with a required remediation date of May 3, 2022.

associated_actors.description: APT19 (Codoso) is a Chinese cyber espionage group that Mandiant Threat Intelligence has tracked since at least 2010 when the group targeted the website of the Nobel Peace Prize. They are relatively sophisticated in comparison with other Chinese operators and on numerous occasions have been linked to zero-day exploits used in wateringhole intrusions as well as direct spear-phishing activity. APT19 (Codoso) has targeted a broad range of victims in the public and private sectors as well as civil society.
associated_actors.name: APT19

associated_actors.description: APT21 is a China-nexus cyber espionage actor that engages in cyber operations where the goal is data theft, possibly focusing on data related to political, economic, and social policy and activities as opposed to Intellectual Property (IP) theft. We believe this is a freelancer group with some nation-state sponsorship located in China. APT21 targeting has focused on multiple foreign governments and non-governmental organizations (NGOs), including government organizations in the United States. The targeting of foreign governments and NGOs is consistent with assessed cyber activities of security organizations within the People's Republic of China (PRC), most notably the Ministry of State Security (MSS). Overall, APT21 targets appear to be those entities that oppose China's political status quo. An analysis of APT21 techniques suggests that another of their focus areas is dissident groups that seek greater autonomy or independence from China, such as those from Tibet or Xinjiang, a province in northwest China heavily populated by the Turkic Uyghur ethnic minority, long oppressed by the PRC.
associated_actors.name: APT21

associated_actors.description: APT26 is a cyber espionage group with a China nexus. This group has targeted organizations headquartered in countries including the United States and the United Kingdom. Organizations targeted by APT26 fall into multiple industries, including construction and engineering, aerospace and defense, and high-tech. We suspect APT26 actors target these industries to support both China's military and economic modernization efforts through collection of information that saves time and money that might otherwise need to be spent on research and development programs. This threat group frequently uses strategic web compromises (SWCs) to gain access to target networks and custom backdoors once they are inside a victim environment. Mandiant Threat Intelligence has not observed confirmed APT26 activity since around the time the indictment was filed in mid-2017.
associated_actors.name: APT26

associated_actors.description: APT27 engages in cyber operations where the goal is data theft, including intellectual property theft of data and projects that make a particular organization competitive within its field. This group has targeted multiple organizations headquartered around the globe, including North and South America, Europe, and the Middle East. These organizations fall into a range of different industries, including business services, high tech, government, and energy; however a notable number are in the aerospace and transport or travel industries. Based on available data, we assess that this is a China-based threat group, possibly a freelancer group with some nation-state sponsorship.
associated_actors.name: APT27

associated_actors.description: APT32 is an espionage operation aligned with the national interests of Vietnam. In addition to focused targeting businesses and industries with interests in the country, the group has also targeted foreign governments and Vietnamese dissidents and journalists consistent with the interests of the state.
associated_actors.name: APT32

associated_actors.description: APT28 is a cyber espionage group with a nexus to Russia that has employed a variety of methodologies and malware to include spear phishing, watering holes, credential collection and the exploitation of mobile platforms in the execution of global espionage campaigns. APT28 campaign targets indicate specific interest in the collection of information intended to provide political and military advantage. These operations have been detected primarily impacting entities across the public and private sector in the US, Europe, Norway and Japan. However, open-source reporting suggests targeting of government and military targets in other regions, including South America, the Middle East and entities in Mexico and Turkey.
associated_actors.name: APT28

associated_actors.description: APT37 is a cyber espionage group that we assess carries out operations on behalf of the North Korean government given malware development artifacts and targeting that aligns with North Korean state interests. APT37 has likely been active since at least 2012 and focuses on targeting the public and private sector primarily in South Korea. In 2017, APT37 expanded its targeting beyond the Korean peninsula and to a wider range of industry verticals, including chemicals, electronics, manufacturing, aerospace, automotive, and healthcare entities in terms of both geography and sector.
associated_actors.name: APT37

associated_actors.description: APT36 is a long-standing cyber espionage actor that conducts intelligence collection in support of Pakistani military and diplomatic interests. Active since at least 2013, APT36 intrusion campaigns reflect a concerted effort to target regional rival India, while also demonstrating an interest in targeting military and intergovernmental organizations such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the United Nations (UN) that have a stake in the region. In addition, APT36 has targeted multiple industries in nations outside of the region to include the U.S. APT36 typically employs spear phishing as a primary method of initial compromise, using malicious attachments that include Microsoft Windows executables and Microsoft Office Documents (that leverage macros and known exploits). This actor's phishing lures usually follow military and political themes. We have further observed these actors leverage a unique watering hole technique that employs social engineering (rather than web exploits) to entice victims to download and open malicious Microsoft Office documents.
associated_actors.name: APT36

associated_actors.description: APT34 is a cyber espionage group with a nexus to Iran that has been operational since at least 2014. We believe APT34 conducts operations largely focused on phishing efforts to benefit Iranian nation-state interests. This threat group has conducted broad targeting across a variety of industries, including financial, government, energy, chemical, and telecommunications, and has largely focused its operations within the Middle East, but has targeted North American and European organizations. We assess that APT34 works on behalf of the Iranian government based on infrastructure details that contain references to Iran, use of Iranian infrastructure, and targeting that aligns with nation-state interests.
associated_actors.name: APT34

associated_actors.description: APT40 is a Chinese cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2013 and has primarily focused on maritime targeting. The group creates infrastructure mimicking U.S. government agencies, defense contractors, and multinational corporations to provide operational relevance and legitimacy. The actors have shifted over to Belt-and-Road Initiative targeting, including targeting regional political and electoral organizations.
associated_actors.name: APT40

associated_actors.description: APT41 is a Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially motivated activity for personal gain. The group has been active since at least 2012 and has conducted espionage operations against healthcare, high-tech, and telecommunications organizations. APT41 also carried out operations against the video game industry for financially motivated intrusions as well as to steal source code and digital certificates. The group executed multiple supply chain compromises, gaining access to software companies to inject malicious code into legitimate files before distributing updates.
associated_actors.name: APT41

associated_actors.description: FIN11 is a financially motivated threat group that has conducted some of the largest and longest running malware distribution campaigns observed amongst our FIN groups to date. Mandiant has observed FIN11 attempt to monetize their operations at least once using named point-of-sale (POS) malware, and more recently using CLOP ransomware and/or data theft extortion. The volume of FIN11's high-volume spam campaigns slowed in 2021, before ceasing altogether in 2022, when the group shifted to server exploitation for initial access. The group has been active since at least 2016, but identified overlaps with activity tracked by security researchers as TA505 suggest they may have been conducting operations as early as 2014.
associated_actors.name: FIN11

associated_actors.description: UNC1014 is a threat cluster active since at least 2017 that has used diversified delivery tactics and zero-day exploits to target international financial institutions with highly tailored phishing campaigns. UNC1014 campaigns have delivered NetWire packaged with Powercat, the MacOS version of NetWire, and/or the Mokes trojan. UNC1014 has monetized intrusions via the theft of cryptocurrency.
associated_actors.name: UNC1014

associated_actors.description: UNC1078 is a threat cluster that has distributed malicious documents crafted to download multi-stage PowerShell scripts ultimately leading to the execution of BEACON or REDZONE. Scripts and secondary payloads distributed by these malicious documents have been hosted on either Github or spoofed infrastructure. Based on targeting similarities to other Chinese groups, we suspect the activity is being conducted by suspected Chinese operators.
associated_actors.name: UNC1078

associated_actors.description: UNC1172 is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group characterize by spear-phishing campaigns targeting the Tibetan Government and the Tibetan diaspora in Europe. The group has also targeted international broadcast corporations and used FIRESHADOW in its operations. We believe the group has been active since at least 2018.
associated_actors.name: UNC1172

associated_actors.description: UNC1151 is a suspected Belarusian cyber espionage group. UNC1151 has targeted a wide variety of governmental and private sector entities, with a focus in Ukraine, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, and Germany. The targeting also includes Belarusian dissidents, media entities, and journalists. UNC1151 uses credential harvesting domains attempting to spoof legitimate webmail providers, generic login pages, and the legitimate websites of their targets. UNC1151 has used a proprietary suite of malware, including HIDDENVALUE, and HALFSHELL, and has infrequently been observed using open source or publicly available tools. UNC1151 has been active since at least 2016.
associated_actors.name: UNC1151

associated_actors.description: UNC1189 is a cluster of activity focused on public sector entities in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and possibly the Palestinian Territories. The group primarily relies on publicly available tools, including EMPIRE, EMPYRE, and KOADIC, and has used URL shortening services alongside Arabic-language social engineering content to deliver PIECEMEAL. UNC1189 has targeted entities in the government, hospitality, media, telecommunications, and transportations sectors since late 2017.
associated_actors.name: UNC1189

associated_actors.description: UNC1272 is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group focused on internal stability monitoring and surveillance campaigns in China's periphery. The group has used EGGROLL and FRYCOOK malware alongside BEACON to target the media and entertainment sector in Japan and Hong Kong since at least late 2018. We believe UNC1272 may also have targeted a U.S.-based non-governmental organization and protestors in Hong Kong with EGGROLL malware in late 2018 and 2019.
associated_actors.name: UNC1272

associated_actors.description: UNC215 is a cyberespionage group that supports Chinese economic and political interests. They have used phishing campaigns, watering hole attacks, and web exploits for software like Microsoft Sharepoint to gain access to organizations around the world since at least 2014. They have targeted organizations in the government, technology, telecommunications, defense, finance, entertainment, and health care sectors. We assess with low confidence that UNC215 is associated with APT27.
associated_actors.name: UNC215

associated_actors.description: UNC251 is a cluster of activity which signs its malware with many of the same compromised digital certificates initially used by APT41. The operation also uses many of the same shared malware tools including gh0st RAT, SOGU, POISON IVY, and ZXSHELL, but does not leverage the same tactics, techniques, and procedures observed in other APT41 activity.
associated_actors.name: UNC251

associated_actors.description: UNC3318 is distribution threat cluster that delivers emails with malicious Office document via attachments or downloadable links. The intended payload is downloaded by these documents by leveraging macros or dropping HTA or VBS files. Observed payloads are BEACON and DRIDEX.
associated_actors.name: UNC3318

associated_actors.description: UNC623 is a suspected Chinese espionage group focused on Southeast Asia. The operation has mostly targeted government offices and the financial sector, typically with ENDRANT or tools shared with other Chinese groups including SMALLKING. UNC623 also frequently uses publicly available malware such as BEACON and COBALT.
associated_actors.name: UNC623

associated_actors.description: UNC869 is believed to be a Chinese espionage group which has relied on spear-phishing to deliver the CHAINLNK dropper and ultimately, payloads such as QUASIFOUR and DUOBEAN. The operation has targeted government offices, media, transportation, construction, and telecoms especially in Southeast Asia.
associated_actors.name: UNC869

associated_actors.description: Mandiant Threat Intelligence has observed Russia-nexus TEMP.Armageddon's campaigns since at least 2013. We believe its primary objective is collecting information on Ukrainian national security and law enforcement entities in support of Russia's national interest and focuses exclusively on Ukrainian targets, with a particular interest in the ongoing eastern Ukraine conflict. We believe TEMP.Armageddon will almost certainly continue espionage operations against Ukrainian targets and further develop its technical capability. While TEMP.Armageddon's targeting thus far indicates it is a primary threat to entities in Ukraine, similar groups (such as Sandworm Team) that were initially regionally focused have also targeted entities outside the region. Any entity of potential interest to the Russian Government should be aware of TEMP.Armageddon.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.Armageddon

associated_actors.description: Conimes Team typically targets government and private and public entities in Southeast Asian region and particularly Vietnam. Current targeting, in conjunction with past targeting, which included defense and government targets in the US and Asian Pacific region and dissident activity, suggests a mission aligned with the strategic economic and political interests of China.
associated_actors.name: Conimes Team

associated_actors.description: Conference Crew is the name given to a set of ongoing related malicious cyber activities targeting military and private industry in the U.S. defense and aerospace sector since at least 2011. Targeted social engineering email messages primarily using aerospace and defense-related 'upcoming event' themes or industry publications are the primary methodology used to facilitate infection by ELISE malware variants. Conference Crew has been active outside of the US defense industrial base (DIB), carrying out intrusions in Southeast Asia.
associated_actors.name: Conference Crew

associated_actors.description: TEMP.Katar is an Indian cyber espionage operation observed targeting government, military, and non-profit entities primarily in China and Pakistan, though targeting has extended to Germany, South Korea, the United States of America, Argentina, Sri Lanka, Norway, Belgium, Spain, Tanzania, Bangladesh, Ecuador, Brazil, and Australia. The group has used open-source malware such as QUASARRAT and DARKCOMET in their operations, alongside custom malware such as BREAKDANCE to support intelligence operations against affected victims.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.Katar

associated_actors.description: Molerats (Gaza Cybergang) is a regionally-focused cyber espionage team concentrating campaign intrusion activities against diplomatic, financial, and political/military entities operating or with an interest in the Palestinian Territories. A combination of technical artifacts, targeting patterns, and social engineering themes leads us to believe Molerats has a Palestine nexus. The group appears to focus on information related to political and military issues affecting the Palestinian Territories and the wider Middle East region. This group has primarily targeted Ministries of Foreign Affairs, European missions to Palestine, Middle Eastern government entities, although they have also targeted the journalism sector, banks, and various think tanks.
associated_actors.name: Molerats

associated_actors.description: TEMP.Metastrike (aka Cobalt group) is a financially motivated threat group that has been operating since at least 2016 and has primarily targeted organizations based in former Soviet Union bloc countries. The operator(s) end-stage mission is to steal victim funds via multiple monetization tactics. The attackers have been observed stealing funds by targeting bank processing centers and payment systems, conducting ATM attacks, manipulating card limits, exploiting victim access to the SWIFT network, and working with groups of money mules to cash out compromised funds.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.MetaStrike

associated_actors.description: Cyber espionage activity known as Sandworm Team has historically affected a growing set of verticals since 2009. Sandworm Team mostly targets its victims through weaponized documents delivered via spear-phishing e-mails; however, deviations tailored to industrial targets may exist. Sandworm Team has exhibited considerable skill and used extensive resources when conducting offensive activities. Chiefly characterized by their penchant for the Black Energy malware, Sandworm Team has often retrofitted publicly available malware to assist targeted activity that was notably coupled with a zero-day originally sourced by the group.
associated_actors.name: Sandworm Team

associated_actors.description: TEMP.TruthTeller (aka Silence) is a financially motivated threat group that has been active since at least mid-2016.The group has primarily targeted financial institutions in Russia and other Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries, though organizations in various other countries have also been impacted, indicating a likely expansion in geographic targeting over time. TEMP.TruthTeller leverages spear-phishing emails that mimic legitimate financial institutions and contain malicious attachments that deliver TRUEBOT malware.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.TruthTeller

associated_actors.description: TEMP.Tick is a cyber espionage team that has targeted public and private interests in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly South Korea and Japan, since at least 2009. The group has a primary focus on industries within the Asia-Pacific region that make significant investments into research and development, offering the opportunity for theft of sensitive intellectual property. Coupled with its apparent interest in Chinese dissident organizations, TEMP.Tick is highly capable of carrying out a dynamic mission and typically monitors the Asia-Pacific landscape to successfully compromise relevant victims within their mission set.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.Tick

associated_actors.description: TEMP.Trident is a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage actor, primarily known for its use of ICEFOG malware, which has targeted the banking and government sectors since at least January 2018. The 2018 campaign used malicious RTF documents to exploit two vulnerabilities (CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2012-0158) to compromise network systems with signature ICEFOG malware. The documents were likely delivered via targeted e-mail attachments to intended victims in Russia, Turkey, and Central and Southeast Asia, based on malware distribution data. There is some indication the campaign may also extend to Uzbekistan given associated callback infrastructure.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.Trident

associated_actors.description: TEMP.Zagros (aka MuddyWater) is characterized by the use of POWERSTATS, SMUGPIGEON, and MORIAGENT malware typically distributed in conjunction with malicious emails. Active since at least May 2017, TEMP.Zagros targeting is prolific and widespread, having affected multiple industries throughout the Middle East and Central and South Asia, including government, defense, telecommunications, energy, and finance. Targeting patterns and related lures demonstrate a strong focus on targets with a geopolitical nexus and the telecommunications sector in Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. This targeting causes us to assess with moderate confidence that this activity has a nexus to Iran.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.Zagros

associated_actors.description: UNC1069 is a suspected North Korean financial crime group, which may be related to APT38 with low confidence. UNC1069 has targeted a variety of financial services firms and cryptocurrency exchanges. UNC1069 commonly uses spear-phishing that leads to a LONEJOGGER shortcut file, which can lead to UNC1069s non-public implants such as LONERUNNER, WHITEHAUL, or POWERHOUSE. UNC1069 has been active since at least 2018.
associated_actors.name: UNC1069

associated_actors.description: TEMP.Hermit is a cluster of North Korean cyber activity that has been active since at least 2013. The group has significant malware overlaps with other North Korean operators and is believed to share resources such as code and complete malware tools with other distinct actors. While observed TEMP.Hermit activity primarily targets entities in South Korea, it has also targeted other organizations worldwide. TEMP.Hermit's operations closely mirror Pyongyang's immediate geopolitical aims, including prolific espionage campaigns against government offices and defense companies, retaliatory destructive attacks against perceived enemies of the North Korean state, and financially-motivated campaigns against cryptocurrency-related businesses.
associated_actors.name: TEMP.Hermit

associated_actors.description: UNC2464 is believed to be an India-based threat cluster that conducts espionage operations. Elements of this threat cluster align with activity publicly reported as â 80 9cBitter.â 80 9d UNC2464 has targeted the South Asian government sector as well as Chinese nuclear research entities and typically leverages spear phishing as a means to deploy malware.
associated_actors.name: UNC2464

associated_actors.description: UNC2063 is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group known to have targeted South and Southeast Asian governments as well as entities in the oil and gas, construction and engineering, manufacturing, and energy sectors since 2018. The group uses a combination of shared and publicly available tools alongside custom malware such as MIGHTYPING and WAVEMINE.
associated_actors.name: UNC2063

associated_actors.description: APT43 is a prolific cyber operator that supports the interests of the North Korean regime. The group combines moderately-sophisticated technical capabilities with aggressive social engineering tactics, especially against South Korean and US-based government organizations, academics, and think tanks focused on Korean peninsula geopolitical issues. In addition to its espionage campaigns, we believe APT43 funds itself through cyber-crime operations to support its primary mission of collecting strategic intelligence. The group creates numerous spoofed and fraudulent personas for use in social engineering, as well as cover identities for purchasing operational tooling and infrastructure. APT43 has collaborated with other North Korean espionage operators on multiple operations, underscoring the major role APT43 plays in the regimeâ 80 99s cyber apparatus.
associated_actors.name: APT43

associated_actors.description: UNC2970 is a suspected North Korean-sponsored threat cluster that has targeted multiple US organizations using targeted spear phishing emails, of which at least one included a job recruitment theme. The threat cluster employs the PLANKWALK backdoor, among other malware families, that shares code with multiple tools leveraged by TEMP.Hermit.
associated_actors.name: UNC2970

associated_actors.description: APT38 is a financially motivated North Korean regime-backed group responsible for conducting destructive attacks against financial institutions, as well as some of the world's largest cyber heists. Based on widely publicized operations alone, the group has attempted to steal more than $1.1 billion.
associated_actors.name: APT38

associated_malware.description: DADSTACHE is a lightweight backdoor written in C++ that communicates via HTTP. It supports the creation of a reverse shell and file transfer.
associated_malware.name: DADSTACHE

associated_malware.description: COLDROCK is a backdoor that has been observed being dropped by an exploit document. The backdoor is capable of gathering system information and sending back the GUID in the initial traffic to the C&C server.
associated_malware.name: COLDROCK

associated_malware.description: BREEZESUGAR is a downloader written in C++ that retrieves a payload via HTTP. The payload is written to disk and persistence is established for it. The persistence method varies based on the OS version. BREEZESUGAR uploads basic system information when requesting a payload. The uploaded information includes installed applications, enumerated logical drives, the system name, and the OS version.
associated_malware.name: BREEZESUGAR

associated_malware.description: DADJOKE is a downloader written in C++ that communicates via HTTP. Retrieved payloads are mapped directly into memory and executed.
associated_malware.name: DADJOKE

associated_malware.description: EIGHTBALL is suspected of being used by the government of India to target Pakistan and internal threats. The EIGHTBALL ecosystem consists of two stages where exploit documents are used to download the EIGHTBALL backdoor.
associated_malware.name: EIGHTBALL

associated_malware.description: DARKCHEESE is backdoor written in C and modified from PCShare. It is capable of sending system information to C&C server and manipulating files.
associated_malware.name: DARKCHEESE

associated_malware.description: FOCUSFJORD is a downloader written in C and assembly that retrieves shellcode payloads via HTTPS or a custom binary protocol over TCP. Payloads are written to disk or injected into a running process prior to execution. FOCUSFJORD is frequently launched via DLL search-order hijacking.
associated_malware.name: FOCUSFJORD

associated_malware.description: BUSTEDROAD is a dropper written in C/C++ that writes an embedded payload to disk and establishes persistence for the payload via the registry. The dropper does not execute the payload. BUSTEDROAD has been observed dropping multiple malware families including CLUBHOUSE, COLDPOT, KNOLLFIDDLER, REDHAWK, and TRIPMISS.
associated_malware.name: BUSTEDROAD

associated_malware.description: GRAPHRAFT is a downloader written in C/C++ that retrieves a shellcode payload via HTTP. The payload is executed directly in memory. GRAPHRAFT has been observed determining the IP address of its remote server using Cloudflare's DNS over HTTPS (DoH) service.
associated_malware.name: GRAPHRAFT

associated_malware.description: FIRESHADOW is a backdoor written in C++ that communicates via SSL over TCP. Supported commands include reverse shell creation, screenshot capture, file transfer, file execution, and uninstall. FIRESHADOW can also enumerate files and collect system information including running processes and installed applications.
associated_malware.name: FIRESHADOW

associated_malware.description: ICEFOG.m is a variant of ICEFOG discovered in 2019 that become file-less and communicates through HTTPS.
associated_malware.name: ICEFOG.M

associated_malware.description: LIGHTSERVER.v2 is a variant of the LIGHTSERVER backdoor. It is capabable of gathering system information, downloading and deleting files, manipulating system settings, and connecting to multiple hard-coded command and control (C&C) servers, and updating its configuration.
associated_malware.name: LIGHTSERVER.V2

associated_malware.description: LEMUR is a dropper that will load an embedded executable and beacon to a C&C server. Previous C&C responses returned encrypted shellcode. LEMUR has been previously observed launched from APT32 lure documents.
associated_malware.name: LEMUR

associated_malware.description: HAWKBALL is a backdoor that is capable of surveying the host, creating a named pipe to execute native windows commands, terminating processes, creating, deleting, and uploading of files, searching for files, and enumerating drives. Prior to execution HAWKBALL checks if it is being debugged and will spawn a mutex to prevent multiple instances from launching.
associated_malware.name: HAWKBALL

associated_malware.description: HAIRBALL is a delphi backdoor related to Dark Caracal.
associated_malware.name: HAIRBALL

associated_malware.description: LOTUSGHOST is shellcode that downloads a payload via HTTP and executes it in memory. Observed payloads have been retrieved from legitimate hosting services including Google Drive and Amazon AWS S3.
associated_malware.name: LOTUSGHOST

associated_malware.description: SADWISH.V2 is a lightweight backdoor written in C++ that communicates via HTTP. SADWISH.V2 executes a file or shell command provided by its C2 server. The results of execution may be uploaded to the C2 server. SADWISH.V2 includes changes to the backdoor's configuration structure and decryption routine.
associated_malware.name: SADWISH

associated_malware.description: KAYSLICE is a downloader that downloads an encrypted payload over SSL from a configured command and control server.
associated_malware.name: KAYSLICE

associated_malware.description: RIGHTSIDE is a backdoor written in C/C++ that communicates via a custom binary protocol over TCP. Supported backdoor commands include keystroke capture, reverse shell, file transfer, file execution, registry manipulation, and service manipulation. RIGHTSIDE can also download and execute payloads via HTTP. Captured keystrokes are written to a file.
associated_malware.name: RIGHTSIDE

associated_malware.description: Icefog Trojan variants include versions for Windows and Mac OS X that can steal information, download and execute programs, execute system commands, and interface with MSSQL servers. Newer versions can use a proxy for their command and control (C&C) communications. Each of these variants may leverage different persistence mechanisms or perform C&C communications using a variety of protocols like SMTP, HTTP, or a custom protocol over TCP Port 5600.
associated_malware.name: ICEFOG

associated_malware.description: AGENTTESLA is a .NET-based credential stealer capable of capturing keystrokes, clipboard data, camera images, and screenshots. AGENTTESLA also targets credentials stored by applications that include web browsers, FTP clients, and email clients. AGENTTESLA can be configured to exfiltrate data via HTTP, SMTP, FTP, Telegram, or a downloaded Tor proxy utility. Some variants may be configured to propagate via USB drives.
associated_malware.name: AGENTTESLA

associated_malware.description: METALJACK is a backdoor written in C++ that initially communicates via DNS or HTTP. The DNS or HTTP response contains the IP address of a true C2 server used for subsequent communication via a custom binary protocol over TCP. Supported backdoor commands include file execution, filesystem manipulation, and registry manipulation.
associated_malware.name: METALJACK

associated_malware.description: POWERSTATS is a nonpublic PowerShell-based first stage backdoor primarily deployed against targets in the Middle East.
associated_malware.name: POWERSTATS

associated_malware.description: LightServer is capable of gathering system information, downloading and deleting files, manipulating system settings, connecting to multiple hard-coded command and control (C&C) servers, and updating its configuration. It is dropped as a .DLL file and uses a text-based file with a non-standard extension to store configuration information. This Trojan maintains persistence by editing the äóìRunäó 9d key in the registry.
associated_malware.name: LIGHTSERVER

associated_malware.description: KNOLLFIDDLER is a downloader that sends and receives data as referral headers. The data is encoded with a multi-byte XOR key, encrypted with RC4, and finally base64 encoded. The malware is capable of sending a host survey and downloading and executing additional payloads.
associated_malware.name: KNOLLFIDDLER

associated_malware.description: LEFTOUT is a dropper for the RIGHTSIDE malware, which it decodes from its resources using a specific XOR-decoding routine. It checks for certain AV processes and launches a legitimate binary to side-load RIGHTSIDE.
associated_malware.name: LEFTOUT

associated_malware.description: SODARIVER is a downloader capable of downloading a second stage payload from a C&C server whose IP address is preconfigured inside the malware. Traffic from the downloader mimics a normal image download.
associated_malware.name: SODARIVER

associated_malware.description: METASTAGE is a small shellcode binary from the Metasploit toolkit known as 'reverse_https stager.' METASTAGE typically gets unpacked by a parent executable, which is packed in several stages. The outer layer of the parent file contains strings and some code to make it look like an innocuous test application. The parent file unpacks METASTAGE shellcode and executes it, which downloads a secondary payload that gets loaded into memory and executed.
associated_malware.name: METASTAGE

associated_malware.description: HALFBAKED is a backdoor written in VBScript that communicates via HTTP. The backdoor's capabilities include screenshot capture, file download, file execution, process enumeration, system information collection, and self-update.
associated_malware.name: HALFBAKED

associated_malware.description: CMDEXE (cmd.exe) is the Windows command shell
associated_malware.name: CMDEXE

associated_malware.description: SOFTSLING is a backdoor capable of collecting a victim survey, performing file operations such as reading, writing, deleting, and executing files, folders and drives, establishing a reverse shell, and terminating processes.
associated_malware.name: SOFTSLING

associated_malware.description: TRUTHTREE is a backdoor written in C++ that communicates via a custom binary protocol over TCP. Supported commands include reverse shell creation, file transfer and management, and shell command execution. The backdoor can also interact with the registry, manipulate processes, and collect basic system information.
associated_malware.name: TRUTHTREE

associated_malware.description: xRAT malware is an open source backdoor coded in C# (using .NET framework 2.0). xRAT supports file management, task management, remote desktop, reverse shell, and the upload and download of files. The backdoor communicates using a custom binary protocol with AES encryption and LZ4 compression. XRAT also encrypts the values in its configuration and does not set persistence. xRAT was renamed to Quasar (QUASARRAT) by the developers in August 2015.
associated_malware.name: XRAT

associated_malware.description: NJRAT is a .NET-based backdoor that communicates using a custom text-based protocol over TCP. Its core functionality involves expanding its capabilities by retrieving plugins from a C2 server. The backdoor's capabilities include video capture, audio capture, screenshot capture, keystroke capture, reverse shell creation, file transfer, file execution, credential theft, and propagation via USB drive.
associated_malware.name: NJRAT

associated_malware.description: SOURDROP is an in-memory dropper written in C++ that executes an embedded payload in memory. Observed payloads include POISONIVY, SOGU and FIRESHADOW.
associated_malware.name: SOURDROP

associated_malware.description: ThreadKit is a builder program written in python to generate malicious RTF documents. The malicious documents exploit one or more vulnerabilities, when opened with vulnerable versions of Microsoft Office, to try to execute a malicious payload.
associated_malware.name: THREADKIT

associated_malware.description: LOKIBOT is a credential stealer written in C/C++ that targets credentials for numerous applications including web browsers, password managers, email clients, and FTP clients. It is also capable of collecting cryptocurrency wallets, capturing keystrokes, and retrieving additional payloads. Harvested data is uploaded via HTTP.
associated_malware.name: LOKIBOT

associated_malware.description: SEEDOOR is a .NET-based backdoor that communicates using a custom binary protocol over TCP. Supported backdoor commands include arbitrary shell command execution, file transfer, and file execution. SEEDOOR can also be tasked with capturing microphone audio, keystrokes, and screenshots.
associated_malware.name: SEEDOOR

associated_malware.description: URSNIF is an ecosystem of related backdoors written in C/C++ that communicate via HTTP. The URSNIF.LDR4 variant of this malware is a significant rewrite and simplification of URSNIF.RM3, losing its banking trojan functionality to intercept and modify web traffic and instead being refocused to deliver secondary payloads. Earlier variants of the malware including URSNIF.RM3 had a broad range of functionality and a modular architecture that enabled the malware to log keystrokes, capture screenshots and clipboard data, extract credentials from installed software, and act as a proxy server.
associated_malware.name: URSNIF

associated_malware.description: REVENGERAT is a .NET-based backdoor that communicates using a custom text-based protocol over TCP. Supported backdoor commands include remote desktop, credential theft, reverse shell creation, keystroke capture, clipboard capture, and file execution. REVENGERAT can also be used to manage services, files, registry items, and processes.
associated_malware.name: REVENGERAT

associated_malware.description: WORDMOPPER is a dropper written in C++. Embedded payloads may be injected into a suspended process or written to a file prior to execution. Observed embedded payloads include the FIRESHADOW backdoor.
associated_malware.name: WORDMOPPER

associated_malware.description: REMCOS is a backdoor written in C++ that communicates using a custom binary protocol over TCP. Supported backdoor commands include mouse and keyboard manipulation, arbitrary shell command execution, file transfer, and file execution. REMCOS can also capture webcam video, microphone audio, keystrokes, and screenshots.
associated_malware.name: REMCOS

associated_malware.description: UPDATESEE is a .NET-based downloader that retrieves payloads via a custom binary protocol over TCP. The downloaded payload is written to disk before it is executed. UPDATESEE has been observed downloading the SEEDOOR backdoor.
associated_malware.name: UPDATESEE

associated_malware.description: SADWISH is a Windows x86 backdoor, sometimes found packed with Enigma Protector. The malware communicates via HTTP to a hard-coded C&C in an embedded and encrypted configuration.
associated_malware.name: SADWISH.V2

associated_malware.description: QUASARRAT is a publicly available Windows backdoor. It may visit a website, download, upload, and execute files. QUASARRAT may acquire system information, act as a remote desktop or shell, or remotely activate the webcam. The backdoor may also log keystrokes and steal passwords from commonly used browsers and FTP clients. QUASARRAT was originally named xRAT before it was renamed by the developers in August 2015.
associated_malware.name: QUASARRAT

associated_malware.description: POISONIVY is a backdoor that exists as shellcode and communicates via a custom binary protocol over TCP. Additional shellcode plugins are downloaded, mapped directly into memory, and executed. Observed plugin functionality includes reverse shell, keylogging, video capture, audio capture, and registry manipulation. POISONIVY is configured, built, and controlled using a publicly available management interface. The interface produces the shellcode that must be included in, or executed by, a separate application.
associated_malware.name: POISONIVY

associated_malware.description: SOGU is a backdoor written in C. The network protocol varies between samples and may include HTTP, HTTPS, a custom binary protocol over TCP or UDP, and ICMP. Supported commands include file transfer, file execution, remote desktop, screenshot capture, reverse shell, and keylogging.
associated_malware.name: SOGU

associated_malware.description: PHISHERY is a Simple SSL Enabled HTTP server with the primary purpose of phishing credentials via Basic Authentication. PHISHERY also provides the ability easily to inject the URL into a .docx Word document.
associated_malware.name: PHISHERY

associated_malware.description: SHORTCUT is a publicly available utility that allows you to create, modify or query Windows shell links (shortcuts) from the command-line. You can export the properties of an existing shortcut to a text file in .INI format.
associated_malware.name: SHORTCUT

associated_malware.description: Impacket is a Python library that allows users to work with various network protocols.
associated_malware.name: IMPACKET

raw_data.description:
Microsoft's Word is a component of the Microsoft Office Suite. Word provides advanced text editing functionality for a wide variety of file formats, including Word Document (.doc), Rich Text File (.rtf) and HTML (.htm).

A vulnerability exists within the parsing of RTF document files in Word due to a mishandling of data within the Windows Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) feature.
raw_data.executive_summary: An input validation vulnerability exists in the parsing of olelink objects in Office RTF files in Microsoft Word 2016 and earlier that, when exploited, allows an attacker to remotely execute arbitrary code. Exploit code is publicly available, and a detailed write-up is available that outlines the required steps of setting up a malicious RTF file. Exploitation activity has been observed in the wild. Mitigation options include a vendor fix. Exploitation Rating: Confirmed

title: Microsoft Word 2016 olelink Object Handling Input Validation Vulnerability
description:
Microsoft's Word is a component of the Microsoft Office Suite. Word provides advanced text editing functionality for a wide variety of file formats, including Word Document (.doc), Rich Text File (.rtf) and HTML (.htm).

A vulnerability exists within the parsing of RTF document files in Word due to a mishandling of data within the Windows Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) feature.
executive_summary: An input validation vulnerability exists in the parsing of olelink objects in Office RTF files in Microsoft Word 2016 and earlier that, when exploited, allows an attacker to remotely execute arbitrary code. Exploit code is publicly available, and a detailed write-up is available that outlines the required steps of setting up a malicious RTF file. Exploitation activity has been observed in the wild. Mitigation options include a vendor fix. Exploitation Rating: Confirmed
analysis:
An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code. The attacker would need to specially craft a malicious RTF document file and convince a user to open it. The application may crash during the exploitation attempt resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

 

A detailed write-up outlining the creation of a malicious RTF file is available online. Minimal effort is required to create such an RTF file, which would be executed automatically upon opening the OLE object. In the example it launches a hidden powershell process to connect with Metasploit.

 

Exploit code was released in the form of a Python script. The script acts as a toolkit that can generate a malicious RTF file and host an HTA file on a local instance of Apache Web server for OLE linking in the malicious RTF. User interaction is still required to open the malicious RTF file.

 

Further, a Metasploit module has been added to the Metasploit Framework. The module is capable of creating a specially crafted RTF file. When downloaded and opened or previewed in Microsoft Office products, the vulnerability is triggered and an embedded payload is executed.

 

Exploitation activity was previously reported as being observed in the wild. In addition to that exploitation, FireEye has identified an exploit document which was uploaded from Brazil. It is believed that this document was used to attack Brazil according to it"s submission country and decoy file contents. Upon execution, this malicious file downloads more malicious Macros samples from an external link. The Macros files launches PowerShell commands, which in turn, injects the Revenge RAT malware into a victim"s system.

 

FireEye has recently identified a malicious document that we suspect could have been used to target Argentinian victims. Upon exploitation, it drops a REMCOS RAT (Remote Administration Tool) on a vulnerable host, allowing an attacker to control a victim"s machine.

 

Another malicious .doc file has been identified by FireEye which contains an exploit that is reportedly being used to install Revenge RAT Malware on victim machines. Upon execution, the exploit communicates with a C&C server hosted on a Brazilian IP (187.14.228.49). The Revenge RAT Malware would allow an attacker to remotely control a victimized machine.

 

Actor JackDelta has been reportedly selling an Office Word Exploit Builder with subscription services on multiple hacking related forums under different but similar handlers and posts.

 

Pakistani-linked threat actor APT36 has reportedly exploited this vulnerability as part of an email phishing campaign to distribute Crimson RAT. This campaign has made use of false COVID-19 health advisories that claim to originate from the government of India, with attached Microsoft Office documents containing a Visual Basic payload.

 

Chinese-linked threat actor APT10 has reportedly exploited this vulnerability in conjunction with several others in targeted attacks against government institutions, cloud service providers, and customer networks worldwide.

 

In June 2021, Mandiant observed exploitation of this vulnerability in-the-wild as part of a malicious RTF document containing the POISONSTEEL .NET backdoor as a payload.

 

In October 2021, Mandiant observed exploitation of this vulnerability in the wild as part of a malicious .doc file containing an unidentified dropper.

 

In April 2022, Mandiant observed evidence of exploitation by the DPRK against South Korean targets, making use of malicious .docx files with a Visual Basic payload.

 

Microsoft reportedly addressed this vulnerability in an update. FireEye considers this a High-risk vulnerability due to the potential for arbitrary code execution of a known zero day vulnerability currently being exploited in the wild. Though the vulnerability requires user interaction, it is still being considered High-risk due to the current exploitation activity.

 
 


CISA added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on November 3, 2021, with a required remediation date of May 3, 2022.
